statement: Freshly laid eggs/seeds initially use negligible amounts of dioxygen.

scores.rationale: The corpus contains multiple, mutually consistent statements affirming the stylized fact that freshly laid eggs and seeds initially use negligible dioxygen. This is presented as a core DEB respiration fact (R1/O1) across several foundational sources (Kooijman 2010, Sousa & Domingos 2007/2008/2010, Sous2007, Kooy2012), often with supporting empirical citations (Romijn & Lokhorst 1951; Pettit 1982; Bucher 1983; Whitehead 1987). Snippet 2 explicitly extends the claim to plant seeds. Several snippets are merely topically adjacent (bird-egg O2 diffusion limitation, hypoxia studies, toxicant exposure, yolk-feeding model details) and are scored neutral, but none of the snippets contradict the fact. Overall the evidence is strong and the consensus clearly corroborates the stylized fact.

scores.rationale: None of the snippets directly address the stylized fact that freshly laid eggs/seeds initially consume negligible dioxygen. Most snippets concern egg contaminants (mercury, PCBs, DDE, dioxins), hatchability effects of toxins/antioxidants, or reproductive performance, which are off-topic. A few touch on oxygen tangentially: snippet [2] notes low dissolved oxygen reduces metabolic rates during fruit fly egg storage, snippet [16] discusses hypoxia effects on cowpea bruchid reproduction, and snippet [10] reports reduced oxygen consumption in non-viable heme-depleted eggs—but none measure or describe the time-course of oxygen uptake in freshly laid eggs to confirm or refute initial negligible respiration. Snippet [17] mentions oxidation of organic compounds during incubation but does not characterize the early phase. Therefore the corpus provides no real evidence either supporting or contradicting the fact; evidence is sparse and the direction is effectively neutral/insufficient.
